opus-5.5.text:
I think what I found most illuminating about that figure is that it tells a story, almost like a roadmap. We started from a standard ResNet-50 and asked a very simple question: if we take the design decisions that made Vision Transformers successful and apply them one by one to a pure ConvNet, how far can we go? And the figure lays that out step by step, from changing the training recipe, to the macro design like the stage compute ratio and the "patchify" stem, to using depthwise convolutions and an inverted bottleneck, larger kernel sizes, and then all the micro-level details: swapping ReLU for GELU, using fewer activations and fewer normalization layers, replacing BatchNorm with LayerNorm, separate downsampling layers.

What struck me is that no single change was a magic bullet. Each one gives you a little bit, sometimes half a percent, sometimes less. But when you accumulate them, the ConvNet ends up matching or even surpassing Swin Transformer at a similar compute budget. So the lesson for me was that a lot of the gap people attributed to the attention mechanism itself was actually coming from these many design choices and from the training procedure. The training recipe alone gave a surprisingly big jump, and that was humbling, because it means that when we compare architectures, we're often not comparing them on equal footing.

The other thing I liked is that it is very honest. You can see every step, including the ones that didn't help much, and anyone can follow the trajectory and reproduce it. For me, research like this is less about claiming "ConvNets are better than Transformers" and more about understanding what really matters. The figure kind of demystifies things. It shows that the inductive biases of convolution are still very valuable, and that the field had maybe moved on a bit too quickly without carefully revisiting the baseline.

r001.rationale: The response describes the figure’s step-by-step ablations, but does not say that this controlled-ablation method can transfer to papers on different topics.

fable-5.1.text:
That figure was, honestly, the thing that I think made the paper. We spent a lot of time on it. The idea was very simple: start from a standard ResNet-50, and then step by step, one change at a time, "modernize" it toward the design of a Swin Transformer. And every time we made a change, we trained the whole thing again and reported the ImageNet accuracy, and we also tracked the FLOPs so you can see we weren't just making the model bigger.

What I found illuminating is that when you lay it out this way, there's no single trick. Nobody can point at it and say, "aha, that's the one thing that makes Transformers work." It's the training recipe, it's the stage compute ratio, it's the patchify stem, it's the depthwise convolution and the inverted bottleneck, it's the large kernel size, and then a bunch of these micro-design decisions, GELU instead of ReLU, fewer activations, fewer normalization layers, LayerNorm instead of BatchNorm, separate downsampling layers. Each one gives you a small bump. Some are almost noise. But they accumulate, and at the end you have a pure ConvNet that matches or beats Swin.

And the second thing I liked about it is that it's an honest figure. We showed the steps that didn't help much too. A lot of the time in our field people report the final number, and the story of how you got there disappears. I always tell students, the ablation is the paper. The final number is just the headline. The figure is the argument. It's saying: look, the gap between ConvNets and Transformers that everyone was talking about in 2021 was mostly a gap in design choices and training, not a fundamental gap in the inductive bias of the architecture.

Also, to be honest, the hardest part of making that figure was the ordering. The improvements are not completely independent, so the order you apply them in changes how much credit each one gets. We tried to pick a trajectory that was reasonable and that told a clear story, but we were very explicit in the paper that this is one path, not the only path. I think that honesty is part of why people trusted it.

r001.rationale: The response describes changing one design choice at a time, retraining, and reporting results, and presents ablations as a general argument. It does not clearly say this method transfers to papers on different topics.

astra-6.text:
What I find illuminating is that it turns the comparison into a sequence of concrete design choices. Instead of saying, “Transformers work better than ConvNets,” you ask: which changes actually account for the improvement? How much comes from the training recipe, and how much comes from the architecture?

As you modernize a conventional ConvNet step by step, you see that convolution itself wasn’t necessarily the limitation. A lot of the surrounding design choices deserved to be revisited.

But there’s also a caveat: that kind of ablation is a path through the design space. Each change is measured on top of the previous changes, so its contribution depends on that context. I’d read the figure as evidence that these choices can work together, rather than as a universal ranking of which architectural ingredients matter most.

r001.rationale: The response describes stepwise ablations and notes that their results depend on context, but it does not say the method can transfer to papers on different topics.

sol-6.1.text:
What I found illuminating was that the gap wasn’t simply “convolution versus attention.” Starting from a standard ResNet, we could make a series of changes to the training recipe and architecture and gradually reach the performance of a hierarchical Transformer, while keeping the network fully convolutional.

And the ablations weren’t a story where every change independently made things better. Some choices depended on what we had already changed. That’s an important lesson: architectural decisions interact, so a negative result in one setting doesn’t necessarily mean an idea is bad.

For me, the figure really challenged the assumption that attention itself explained the whole improvement. A lot of progress was also coming from the design choices surrounding it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses interacting architectural choices and challenges the idea that attention explains all gains, but it does not identify the ablation method as transferable to papers on different topics.
